Preparing and cleaning a corpus

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/preparing-corpus.Rmd
preparing-corpus.Rmd

A sentence encoder represents everything in a text, including what an analyst would not count as content. A copyright notice at the end of an abstract, a list marker, a URL or a broken character moves the text’s embedding, and when the same noise recurs across many texts it can draw them together into a topic of its own, grouped by publisher or formatting rather than by meaning. Repetition has a similar effect: a text that occurs two hundred times enters k-means two hundred times and pulls a center toward itself. Corpus preparation therefore precedes encoding, and every step changes the data that are modeled, so each one should be stated and its effect counted.

This guide prepares the covid abstracts in the order the steps should be applied: removing records without text, removing duplicates, repairing and cleaning the text, and checking how much of each unit is prose. Every step runs without a model. Choosing the words that describe topics, which is done after fitting and does not change the text, is covered at the end.

library(sbert)
#> sbert 0.6.0: Sentence-BERT embeddings and topic models in R.
#>   14 pinned models (see models()); default: all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
#>   A model is downloaded only on request, once, and verified by SHA-256.

Data

covid holds 4,170 records of research on COVID-19 and education, children, schools and society, published from 2020 to 2024.

  • Abstract: the text of the abstract; the text to be modeled.
  • Year: the year of publication; carried along with each abstract.

The feedback messages of feedback_translations are used where a step is better shown on short texts.

Which records have no text?

Bibliographic exports fill a missing abstract with a placeholder. In covid it is the string "[No abstract available]":

nrow(covid)
#> [1] 4170
nrow(subset(covid, Abstract == "[No abstract available]"))
#> [1] 323

323 of the 4,170 records have no abstract. The placeholder is a well-formed English phrase, so no cleaning step would remove it, and kept, it would become 323 copies of one text, a topic about nothing. It is removed first:

abstracts <- subset(covid, Abstract != "[No abstract available]")
nrow(abstracts)
#> [1] 3847

How much of the corpus repeats?

dedupe() keeps the first occurrence of every distinct text and counts its occurrences in a new column, n. Given a data frame and the name of its text column, it keeps all columns of the first occurrence:

abstracts <- dedupe(abstracts, column = "Abstract")
nrow(abstracts)
#> [1] 3670
with(abstracts, table(n))
#> n
#>    1    2    4 
#> 3495  174    1

The 3,847 records hold 3,670 distinct abstracts: 3,495 occur once, 174 twice, and one four times, records indexed more than once. Had the placeholder been kept, dedupe() would have reduced it to a single row carrying its count:

subset(dedupe(covid, column = "Abstract"), n > 4, select = c(Year, n))
#>    Year   n
#> 73 2023 323

Given a character vector, dedupe() returns the columns text and n. Repetition is far heavier in the feedback messages, which a generator writes from templates:

messages <- with(feedback_translations, dedupe(translation))
nrow(feedback_translations)
#> [1] 8757
nrow(messages)
#> [1] 8005
head(messages, 3)
#>                                                    text n
#> 1                    Do you know what “one more” means? 2
#> 2 There should be two more in the red than in the blue. 3
#> 3               If it’s not a person, what could it be? 2

The 8,757 messages hold 8,005 distinct texts. Modeling the distinct texts keeps repeated templates from dragging the topic centers, and the counts are not lost: after fitting, topic_sizes(weights = "n") reports every topic’s share of all occurrences beside its share of distinct texts. On the first 600 distinct messages, whose embeddings are bundled:

corpus <- head(dedupe(feedback_translations, column = "translation"), 600)
topic_model <- topics(corpus, n_topics = 6, column = "translation",
                      embeddings = feedback_embeddings)
topic_sizes(topic_model, weights = "n")
#>   topic                                                       label n_documents
#> 1     1   Where is the cow and the cake? Choose all the pictures...         223
#> 2     2            All the ones between the cat and the strawberry.         133
#> 3     3         What does “all the ones between the leaf and the...         131
#> 4     4 Are you sure you have fewer pictures in the red box than...          49
#> 5     5      In the top middle box, it means something is in the...          37
#> 6     6    It is not a person, does not have a hat, and is sitting.          27
#>   proportion n_weighted weighted_share
#> 1     0.3717        267         0.3608
#> 2     0.2217        162         0.2189
#> 3     0.2183        138         0.1865
#> 4     0.0817         76         0.1027
#> 5     0.0617         57         0.0770
#> 6     0.0450         40         0.0541

n_documents and proportion count distinct messages; n_weighted and weighted_share count occurrences. The topic of corrections (topic 4) holds 8.2% of the distinct messages and 10.3% of the occurrences, because its messages were repeated more often than the others.

What does clean_corpus() repair?

clean_corpus() gathers the text-level cleaning that should happen before encoding, so that the same clean text feeds the encoder, the topic terms and the representative texts. Some repairs are always applied: HTML tags and entities are decoded or removed; URLs, DOIs, e-mail addresses and bracketed numeric citations such as [12] are removed; curly quotes, dashes and bullets are normalized; and control, zero-width and replacement characters are dropped. Removing list and section numbering is on by default and can be switched off. Four invented texts show the effect:

examples <- c("<p>Teachers &amp; parents</p> reported higher stress [12].",
              "Data are available at https://doi.org/10.1000/xyz123 for reuse.",
              "1. Aims. 2. Methods. 3. Results.",
              "Section 2.3.1 describes the sample.")
clean_corpus(examples)
#> [1] "Teachers & parents reported higher stress."
#> [2] "Data are available at for reuse."          
#> [3] "Aims. Methods. Results."                   
#> [4] "Section describes the sample."

The markup, the citation, the URL, the list markers and the section number are gone, and the words are kept.

Abstracts also carry text that the generic repairs cannot recognize. In covid almost every abstract ends with a publisher’s copyright notice:

with(abstracts, sum(grepl("©", Abstract)))
#> [1] 3655

3,655 of the 3,670 abstracts contain the copyright sign. The remove argument takes regular expressions, matched case-insensitively, whose matches are deleted before the other steps. The pattern below deletes a notice at the end of an abstract that starts with “©”, “Copyright ©” or “Copyright” and a year, and leaves abstracts that discuss copyright as a subject untouched. Given a data frame and a column, clean_corpus() cleans that column and keeps the other columns aligned:

cleaned <- clean_corpus(abstracts, column = "Abstract",
                        remove = "(copyright:?\\s*(©|\\d{4})|©).{0,1000}$")
nrow(cleaned)
#> [1] 3670
with(cleaned, sum(grepl("©", Abstract)))
#> [1] 0
with(cleaned, sum(grepl("copyright", Abstract, ignore.case = TRUE)))
#> [1] 2

All 3,670 abstracts are kept, none still contains the copyright sign, and the two that still contain the word “copyright” use it as a subject (accessibility and copyright in online teaching; open educational resources free from copyright issues). The cleaning shortens the abstracts:

with(abstracts, summary(nchar(Abstract)))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>     171    1022    1315    1352    1640    5285
with(cleaned, summary(nchar(Abstract)))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>     117     975    1261    1300    1583    5243

The median abstract loses 54 characters, about the length of a copyright line.

Should numbers be removed from the text?

numbers = TRUE and roman_numerals = TRUE remove stand-alone numeric and Roman-numeral tokens from the text. Both are off by default, because the result is no longer a well-formed sentence:

clean_corpus("In 2020, 45 schools closed during phase ii.",
             numbers = TRUE, roman_numerals = TRUE)
#> [1] "In, schools closed during phase."

The sentence loses its year, its count and its phase, and the encoder sees a fragment. Numbers rarely decide what a text is about, but they do clutter the words that describe topics. That is better handled after fitting, with the numbers = "remove" and roman_numerals = "remove" arguments of topics() and terms(), which filter the terms and leave the text and its embedding intact (see Describing and naming topics).

Which list markers are removed?

strip_list_markers(), which clean_corpus() applies by default, removes enumeration markers that stand alone: 1., (i), (a), (1) and Roman-numeral section markers such as II.. It keeps numbers and parentheses that carry content:

strip_list_markers(c("The aims were (i) access and (ii) equity.",
                     "1. Background 2. Methods 3. Results",
                     "The student ranks in the top 20. Good work.",
                     "Smith v. Jones, cited by V. Nabokov in (2020), with (n=100)."))
#> [1] "The aims were access and equity."                            
#> [2] "Background Methods Results"                                  
#> [3] "The student ranks in the top 20. Good work."                 
#> [4] "Smith v. Jones, cited by V. Nabokov in (2020), with (n=100)."

The markers of the first two texts are removed. A number that ends a sentence (“top 20.”), a year or a count in parentheses, a lower-case “v.” and a mid-sentence initial are kept. In the abstracts, parenthesized markers such as (i), (1) or (a) occur in 193 texts before cleaning and in none after:

marker <- "(^|\\s)\\((i|1|a)\\)\\s"
with(abstracts, sum(grepl(marker, Abstract, perl = TRUE)))
#> [1] 193
with(cleaned, sum(grepl(marker, Abstract, perl = TRUE)))
#> [1] 0

How much of each unit is prose?

content_ratio() is the share of a text’s non-space characters that are letters. Prose scores near 1; references, page ranges, tables of numbers and identifiers score low:

content_ratio(c("A real sentence here.",
                "OJ No L 297, 24.11.1979, p. 1.",
                "doi:10.1007/s10639-021-10557-6"))
#> [1] 0.944 0.250 0.133
with(cleaned, summary(content_ratio(Abstract)))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   0.794   0.962   0.969   0.966   0.975   0.992

Every abstract is mostly prose: the lowest ratio is 0.794. The check matters for smaller units. Split into sentences with segment(), the abstracts yield fragments that are not prose at all:

sentences <- with(cleaned, segment(Abstract, level = "sentence"))
nrow(sentences)
#> [1] 28515
knitr::kable(subset(sentences, content_ratio(text) < 0.5,
                    select = c(document_id, text)))
document_id text
319 44 2006.
4374 550 1999.
4379 550 Ylä-Kotola, 679 - 718.
10130 1220 2021;60(9):534-537.].
16883 2048 26..
17050 2070 The significantly predicted equations were as follows: In term of raw scores: Y/ = 75.425 + (-5.180) (X4) + 3.816 (X3) + (-3.465) (X5) + (-2.689) (X7) In term of standard scores: Z/Y = (-0.324) (Z X 4) + 0.280 (Z X 3) + (-0.225) (Z X3) + (-0.165) Z X 7).
19107 2330 2021
19139 2333 2021

Eight of the 28,515 sentences fall below one half: years, page ranges, the remains of a citation, and a regression equation. Each would be embedded as a unit and could join a topic. min_content drops them: clean_corpus(min_content = ) drops whole documents below the ratio, and segment(min_content = ) and topics(min_content = ) drop segments. Splitting documents is covered in Segmenting long documents.

Which words are ignored when topics are described?

Stop words do not change the text or the embeddings. They are removed only when the words that describe each topic are computed. stop_words() returns the default English list, and add and remove adapt it to a corpus:

length(stop_words())
#> [1] 125
head(stop_words(), 10)
#>  [1] "a"       "about"   "after"   "again"   "against" "all"     "am"      "an"     
#>  [9] "and"     "any"
covid_stop_words <- stop_words(add = c("covid", "pandemic"))
length(covid_stop_words)
#> [1] 127

The default list has 125 words. In a corpus selected for COVID-19, the words covid and pandemic occur in most texts and describe no topic, so they are added. The list is passed as topics(stop_words = ) or terms(stop_words = ).

The preparation in one sequence

The full preparation of the abstracts, in order, ends with an encoding step that needs a downloaded model and is not run here:

abstracts <- subset(covid, Abstract != "[No abstract available]")
abstracts <- dedupe(abstracts, column = "Abstract")
abstracts <- clean_corpus(abstracts, column = "Abstract",
                          remove = "(copyright:?\\s*(©|\\d{4})|©).{0,1000}$",
                          min_content = 0.5)
model_download()
topic_model <- topics(abstracts, n_topics = 10, column = "Abstract",
                      stop_words = stop_words(add = c("covid", "pandemic")),
                      numbers = "remove")
topic_sizes(topic_model, weights = "n")
Problem Verb
Placeholder or empty records subset() before anything else
Repeated texts dedupe(), then topic_sizes(weights = "n")
Markup, URLs, citations, broken characters clean_corpus()
Boilerplate such as copyright notices clean_corpus(remove = )
List and section numbering clean_corpus(), strip_list_markers()
Units that are not prose content_ratio(), min_content =
Uninformative words in topic terms stop_words(add = ), numbers = "remove"

The prepared abstracts are modeled in Case study: COVID-19 research abstracts, and choosing the unit of analysis is discussed in Choosing the number of topics and the granularity.
